title: Trump’s Global Campaign Against ‘Radical Left Terrorism’ is Built on a National Security Memo Without Congressional Approval
author: Melinda Hass
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/01/IMG_6773-680x510.jpg)

Photograph by Nathaniel St. Clair

A little-noticed presidential national security directive is now the legal
engine behind a wave of terrorism prosecutions against left-wing protesters.

That domestic campaign now has an international dimension, one that American
officials had been [planning for months](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-
counterterror-officials-plan-antifa-summit-sources-say-2026-03-31/),
culminating on July 16, 2026, when Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s
Ministerial on the Resurgence of Political Terrorism drew [representatives
from more than 65 countries](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/7/16/us-
hosts-global-meet-on-far-left-terror-whos-attending-why-it-matters) to
Washington. The gathering was informally called the “Antifa summit.”

Rubio described antifa-aligned networks as sharing infrastructure across
borders and accused Iran and Cuba of helping bankroll the movement, [without
offering evidence](https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-
spokesperson/2026/07/remarks-at-the-opening-of-the-ministerial-on-the-
resurgence-of-political-terrorism/). The White House declared the summit the
start of an “[unprecedented global
offensive](https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/07/trump-administration-
unleashes-global-campaign-to-crush-radical-left-terrorism/)” against what it
calls “radical left terrorism.”

This offensive is built on the same domestic legal architecture that has now
sent American activists to prison for decades.

That architecture is [National Security Presidential
Memorandum/NSPM-7](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-
actions/2025/09/countering-domestic-terrorism-and-organized-political-
violence/), issued on Sept. 25, 2025, which for the first time appeared to
authorize preemptive law enforcement measures against Americans based not on
whether they are planning to commit violence but for their political or
ideological beliefs.

Nearly a year later, that blueprint has moved from paper into practice.

The Justice Department has built task forces staffed by counterterrorism
prosecutors. The FBI has set up its own [NSPM-7 mission
center](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/19/us/politics/justice-dept-prosecute-
protesters.html) to oversee investigations into left-wing movements, including
a [joint effort with the IRS](https://www.justsecurity.org/136232/antifa-fisa-
section-702-back-door/) to investigate nonprofit groups.

The Justice Department has [used this
machinery](https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/06/prairieland-ice-dhs-
protest-conspiracy-prison-judge-texas-immigration-sentence/) to convict
activists and send some of them to prison for decades.

NSPM-7 was not passed by Congress. It’s a lesser-known tool of executive
power: a presidential memorandum.

As an [international relations
scholar](https://www.spia.pitt.edu/people/melinda-haas) who has studied [U.S.
foreign policy decision-
making](https://direct.mit.edu/isec/article/45/3/122/95272/To-Disclose-or-
Deceive-Sharing-Secret-Information) and [national security
legislation](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/08850607.2022.2119446),
I recognize that presidents can take several types of [executive
actions](https://sgp.fas.org/crs/misc/RS20846.pdf) without legislative
involvement: [executive orders](https://www.federalregister.gov/presidential-
documents/executive-orders), [memoranda and
proclamations](https://www.federalregister.gov/presidential-documents/other-
presidential-documents).

This structure allows the president to direct law enforcement and national
security agencies, with little opportunity for congressional oversight.

**Presidential national security powers**

[Executive
memorandums](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/onpolitics/2017/01/24/executive-
order-vs-presidential-memorandum-whats-difference/96979014/) direct agencies
to prepare reports, implement policies or align programs with the
administration’s priorities. Unlike executive orders, they aren’t required to
be published. When they relate to national security, like NSPM-7, they’re
called [national security directives](https://www.congress.gov/crs-
product/IF11358) – many of which stay classified and [may not be
declassified](https://lawreview.vermontlaw.edu/wp-
content/uploads/2012/02/10-Duncan-Book-2-Vol.-35.pdf) for years or decades.

The stated purpose of NSPM-7 is to counter domestic terrorism and organized
political violence, focusing mainly on perceived threats from the political
left. The memorandum identifies “anti-Christian,” “anti-capitalism” or “anti-
American” views as potential indicators that a group or person will commit
domestic terrorism.

The memorandum claims that political violence originates with “anti-fascist”
groups that hold the following views: “support for the overthrow of the United
States Government; extremism on migration, race, and gender; and hostility
towards those who hold traditional American views on family, religion, and
morality.”

The strategy includes [preemptive
measures](https://www.kenklippenstein.com/p/trumps-nspm-7-labels-common-
beliefs) to disrupt groups before they engage in violent political acts,
empowering multiagency task forces to investigate potential federal crimes
related to radicalization and the groups’ funders. Former Attorney General Pam
Bondi’s [December 2025 implementation
memo](https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/the-bondi-memo-s-quiet-rewriting-
of-domestic-terrorism-rules) went further, ordering a five-year review of
agency files on antifa. [A task
force](https://www.kenklippenstein.com/p/minnesota-antifa-terrorists-charged)
staffed with counterterrorism and organized-crime prosecutors is carrying out
these investigations.

**‘Domestic terrorist organizations’**

The memorandum directs the Department of Justice to focus FBI resources from
approximately 200 [Joint Terrorism Task
Forces](https://www.fbi.gov/investigate/terrorism/joint-terrorism-task-forces)
on investigating “acts of recruiting or radicalizing persons” for the purpose
of “political violence, terrorism, or conspiracy against rights; and the
violent deprivation of any citizen’s rights.”

NSPM-7 also allows the attorney general to propose groups for designation as
“domestic terrorist organizations.” That includes groups that engage in
“organized doxxing campaigns, swatting, rioting, looting, trespass, assault,
destruction of property, threats of violence, and civil disorder.”

Existing laws allow the [secretary of state](https://www.state.gov/foreign-
terrorist-organizations) to designate groups as “foreign terrorist
organizations” that are then subject to financial sanctions.

[But these laws do not permit](https://theconversation.com/the-domestic-
terrorist-designation-wont-stop-extremism-141258) the president to label
domestic groups this way.

That gap hasn’t stopped prosecutions. In Texas, eight defendants tied to a
“[North Texas Antifa Cell](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/leader-antifa-cell-
members-north-texas-sentenced-100-years-prison-terrorist-attack-ice)” were
sentenced in June 2026 for a 2025 armed confrontation at the Prairieland
immigration detention center. One man received 100 years, and [others who
never fired a weapon](https://theintercept.com/2026/06/23/prairieland-texas-
ice-protest-prison-sentences/) still drew decades in prison under terrorism
sentencing guidelines.

In Minnesota, [15 members and
associates](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/15-members-direct-action-minnesota-
minneapolis-based-direct-action-group-antifa-ties) of a group called Direct
Action Minnesota were indicted in June 2026 on conspiracy and assault charges.
A [94-page indictment](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/16/us/minnesota-
immigration-charges-antifa.html) cited behavior such as wearing an “I’m
Antifa!” sweatshirt, possessing a bullhorn or including a devil emoji in a
Signal message.

**Defining terrorism**

NSPM-7 marks a major conceptual shift in U.S. counterterrorism policy,
departing from approaches that primarily targeted foreign threats.

Earlier directives, [dating to Ronald Reagan’s
presidency](https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/public/archives/reference/scanned-
nsdds/nsdd207.pdf), treated terrorism as a global menace countered through
military power and diplomacy. In the 1990s, the Clinton administration
reframed it as a domestic challenge after the [1993 World Trade Center
bombing](https://www.fbi.gov/history/famous-cases/world-trade-center-
bombing-1993) and [1995 Oklahoma City
bombing](https://www.fbi.gov/history/cases-and-criminals/oklahoma-city-
bombing).

After 9/11, the Bush administration fused counterterrorism with national
defense through the [global war on
terrorism](https://www.georgewbushlibrary.gov/research/topic-guides/global-
war-terror). The Obama administration later tried to narrow those powers,
asking whether targeted individuals “[pose a continuing, imminent threat to
U.S. persons](https://irp.fas.org/offdocs/ppd/ppg-procedures.pdf)” — a
standard focused on tactics and capture feasibility, not ideology.

The first Trump administration used a “[travel
ban](https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/executive-
order-protecting-nation-foreign-terrorist-entry-united-states-2/)” against
several [“terror-prone”](https://abcnews.com/Politics/trump-administration-
justifying-list-countries-banned-travel-us/story?id=45143197) countries, while
President Joe Biden redirected focus toward weapons of mass destruction.

Notably, the “domestic terrorist” label itself has rarely produced actual
charges. The State Department designated [four antifa-aligned
groups](https://www.justsecurity.org/136232/antifa-fisa-section-702-back-
door/) as foreign terrorist organizations. But antifa is a [decentralized
movement](https://www.cbsnews.com/minnesota/news/what-is-antifa/), not a
formal group with a roster.

This designation lacks any real legal weight because [U.S. law has no formal
domestic terrorist organization category](https://www.congress.gov/crs-
product/R47885). Creating one risks infringing on First Amendment protected
speech. Domestic terrorism itself is not a chargeable offense.

Prosecutors have instead leaned on older statutes such as [material support
for terrorism](https://www.justsecurity.org/132743/how-a-broadly-defined-
counterterrorism-statute-could-be-abused/) and [conspiracy
laws](https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/06/minneapolis-protest-doj-
ice-indictment-antifa-nspm-dhs/), tools originally built for cases like the
ones above, not protest movements.

**First Amendment rights at risk**

There is no single official definition of terrorism in U.S. law; definitions
vary by purpose – criminal law, intelligence collection, civil liability.

Definitions in all those areas typically focus on identifying [violent or
dangerous acts](https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-
courts/FSupp/999/1/2267352/) done with the intent to intimidate or coerce
civilians or influence government policy.

But more than redefining terrorism, NSPM-7 reorients the machinery of national
security toward the policing of belief.

The First Amendment generally
[prevents](https://www.arnoldporter.com/en/perspectives/blogs/enforcement-
edge/2025/09/turning-counterterrorism-tools-onto-domestic-policy-targets) the
government from punishing people for unpopular opinions. It also protects the
[ability for people to
associate](https://firstamendment.mtsu.edu/article/freedom-of-association/) to
advance public and private ideas [in pursuit of
political](https://firstamendment.mtsu.edu/article/naacp-v-alabama/),
economic, religious or cultural goals.

The directive’s emphasis on ideological orientations – “anti-Christianity,”
“anti-capitalism” and “anti-American” views – as indicators of domestic
terrorism potentially jeopardizes [First Amendment
rights](https://www.acluaz.org/news/first-amendment-101-an-introduction-to-
the-five-freedoms/).

Thirty-one members of Congress [sent a letter to Trump in October
2025](https://pocan.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/pocan.house.gov/files/evo-
media-document/letter-on-nspm-7-to-president-trump.pdf) expressing “serious
concerns” about NSPM-7, warning that it poses “serious constitutional,
statutory and civil liberties risks, especially if used to target political
dissent, protest or ideological speech.”

As [the ACLU warns](https://www.aclu.org/news/national-security/how-
nspm-7-seeks-to-use-domestic-terrorism-to-target-nonprofits-and-activists),
any definition of terrorism that includes ideological components risks
criminalizing people or groups based on belief rather than based on violence
or other criminal conduct.

[Congress has declined](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47885) to create
a domestic complement to the foreign terrorist designation in large part
because of the potential for impinging on First Amendment–protected
association and speech.

But I fear that chilling speech may be the point.

**Silencing dissent**

NSPM-7 does not criminalize previously legal conduct.

Rather, it states that the Trump administration will focus investigations
around the [identity and ideology of supposed
perpetrators](https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/the-situation--the-
nonsense-and-the-menace). [Prioritizing
investigations](https://the1a.org/segments/if-you-can-keep-it-trump-hate-
speech-and-free-speech/) into this broad swath of ideologies serves to instill
fear, silencing [anti-fascist and other messages in opposition to the Trump
administration](https://theintercept.com/2025/11/04/trump-terrorist-list-
nspm7-enemies/).

Law professor [Steve
Vladeck](https://www.stevevladeck.com/p/bonus-180-domestic-terrorism-and)
frames this chill as “obeying in advance,” in which organizations self-censor
rather than risk investigation, prosecution or defending against the “domestic
terrorist” label. Federal judges in the [Prairieland
case](https://theintercept.com/2026/06/23/prairieland-texas-ice-protest-
prison-sentences/) have shown little sympathy for that distinction: One judge
described the protest itself as “an assault on democracy,” even for defendants
who never touched a weapon.

Although left-wing violence has risen in the past decade, [empirical
evidence](https://www.csis.org/analysis/ideological-trends-us-terrorism) shows
it remains far below historical levels of right-wing or jihadist violence.

Most domestic terrorists in the U.S. [are politically on the
right](https://theconversation.com/right-wing-extremist-violence-is-more-
frequent-and-more-deadly-than-left-wing-violence-what-the-data-shows-265367),
accounting for the vast majority of domestic terrorism fatalities.

Yet NSPM-7 focuses disproportionately on left-wing ideologies. NSPM-7 departs
from prior U.S. counterterrorism frameworks by prioritizing the suppression of
ideologically motivated dissent, even where, as in Minnesota, [judges have
already dismissed](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/16/us/minnesota-
immigration-charges-antifa.html) roughly half of similar federal cases for
lack of evidence.
